claim: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States.
source: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, 2013

claim: Altered blood flow characteristics play a critical role in the focal nature of atherosclerosis.
source: Altered blood flow characteristics (unidirectional vs. disturbed flow) and associated changes in flow-generated mechanical forces (hemodynamics) play a critical role in the focal nature of atherosclerosis (Davies et al., 2013; Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Davies et al., 2013; Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014

claim: Unidirectional blood flow is athero-protective and promotes a healthy endothelium characterized by endothelial cell quiescence and maintenance of vascular barrier integrity.
source: Unidirectional blood flow (UF) is associated with high time-averaged shear stress and is 'athero-protective' promoting a healthy endothelium, characterized by endothelial cell quiescence and maintenance of vascular barrier integrity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Disturbed flow is athero-susceptible and promotes endothelial cell activation characterized by inflammation and reduced vascular barrier integrity.
source: In contrast, disturbed flow (DF), which occurs in areas where atherosclerosis develops, is associated with low time-averaged shear stress and is 'athero-susceptible' promoting EC 'activation' characterized by inflammation and reduced vascular barrier integrity (Davies et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2004; Chiu and Chien, 2011; Liao, 2013; Abe and Berk, 2014; Xiao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Davies et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2004; Chiu and Chien, 2011; Liao, 2013; Abe and Berk, 2014; Xiao et al., 2013

claim: Areas where endothelial cells are subjected to disturbed flow are the branched and curved parts of the arterial tree.
source: These areas where ECs are subjected to DF are the branched and curved parts of the arterial tree and underscores the focal, flow-dependent nature of endothelial 'activation'.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Flow-dependent harbingers of atherosclerosis develop before any visible signs of disease.
source: These flow-dependent harbingers of atherosclerosis develop before any visible signs of disease (Hajra et al., 2000; Won et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hajra et al., 2000; Won et al., 2007

claim: When cultured under static conditions, endothelial cells exhibit increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: When cultured under static conditions, ECs exhibit increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reduced nitric oxide production (Kizhakekuttu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2010; Eelen et al., 2015), and a shift towards glycolysis (Eelen et al., 2015; De Bock et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kizhakekuttu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2010; Eelen et al., 2015

claim: Static culture conditions cause endothelial cells to shift towards glycolysis.
source: When cultured under static conditions, ECs exhibit increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reduced nitric oxide production (Kizhakekuttu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2010; Eelen et al., 2015), and a shift towards glycolysis (Eelen et al., 2015; De Bock et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eelen et al., 2015; De Bock et al., 2013a

claim: Unidirectional flow reduces glycolysis in a KLF2-dependent manner compared to static conditions.
source: Compared to static conditions, UF reduces glycolysis in a Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2)-dependent manner (Dekker et al., 2002; Doddaballapur et al., 2015) and increases mitochondrial biogenesis (Chen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014) but whether UF alters mitochondrial function is controversial (Doddaballapur et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dekker et al., 2002; Doddaballapur et al., 2015

claim: Unidirectional flow increases mitochondrial biogenesis compared to static conditions.
source: Compared to static conditions, UF reduces glycolysis in a Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2)-dependent manner (Dekker et al., 2002; Doddaballapur et al., 2015) and increases mitochondrial biogenesis (Chen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014) but whether UF alters mitochondrial function is controversial (Doddaballapur et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014

claim: Whether unidirectional flow alters mitochondrial function is controversial.
source: Compared to static conditions, UF reduces glycolysis in a Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2)-dependent manner (Dekker et al., 2002; Doddaballapur et al., 2015) and increases mitochondrial biogenesis (Chen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014) but whether UF alters mitochondrial function is controversial (Doddaballapur et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doddaballapur et al., 2015

claim: The effect of physiological disturbed flow on cellular metabolism is unclear.
source: Furthermore, the effect of physiological DF, as opposed to no flow, on cellular metabolism is unclear and the mechanisms behind these DF-induced changes remain under-explored (De Bock et al., 2013a; Doddaballapur et al., 2015; Cucullo et al., 2011; Wilhelm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Bock et al., 2013a; Doddaballapur et al., 2015; Cucullo et al., 2011; Wilhelm et al., 2016

claim: Disturbed flow induces a metabolic phenotype of increased glycolysis and reduced oxidative phosphorylation compared to unidirectional flow.
source: We show that DF induces a metabolic phenotype of increased glycolysis and reduced oxidative phosphorylation, compared to UF.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study

claim: RNA-seq analyses predicted HIF-1α as a major transcriptional regulator controlling disturbed flow-induced changes in endothelial phenotypes.
source: Our RNA-seq analyses predicted HIF-1α as a major transcriptional regulator controlling the DF-induced changes in endothelial phenotypes.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis using IPA

claim: Disturbed flow activates HIF-1α via induction of NOX4 and consequent production of ROS.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that DF activates hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) via induction of NAD(P)H Oxidase-4 (NOX4) and consequent production of ROS.
evidence: Stated as a mechanistic finding from the study

claim: HIF-1α is required for disturbed flow-induced metabolic reprogramming characterized by increased glycolysis and repression of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Activation of HIF-1α was required for DF-induced metabolic reprogramming characterized by increased glycolysis and repression of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation due to inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) via increased pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase-1 (PDK1) expression.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study

claim: HIF-1α increases PDK1 expression, which reduces mitochondrial respiratory capacity under disturbed flow.
source: Activation of HIF-1α was required for DF-induced metabolic reprogramming characterized by increased glycolysis and repression of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation due to inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) via increased pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase-1 (PDK1) expression.
evidence: Stated as a mechanistic finding from the study

claim: Reversal of disturbed flow-induced metabolic reprogramming reduced endothelial activation.
source: Reversal of DF-induced metabolic reprogramming reduced endothelial activation.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 3757 differentially expressed genes between disturbed flow and unidirectional flow using a false discovery rate cutoff of q < 0.05.
source: Analysis of RNA sequencing identified a total of 3757 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) using a false discovery rate cut off value of q < 0.05.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Cellular response to hypoxia and glycolytic metabolism were the most up-regulated gene sets under disturbed flow.
source: Among these pathways, the cellular response to hypoxia and glycolytic metabolism were the most up-regulated gene sets under disturbed flow (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Glucose metabolism and response to hypoxia were among the top 10 gene ontology biological processes induced by disturbed flow.
source: Functional analysis of the RNA-seq data using DAVID (the Database for Annotation, Visualization, and Integrated Discovery) (Huang et al., 2009a), showed that glucose metabolism and response to hypoxia were among the top 10 gene ontology (GO) biological processes induced by DF (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on DAVID analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Unidirectional flow had no effect on hypoxia and glycolysis pathways.
source: In contrast, UF had no effect on these pathways (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Based on pathway analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: Hypoxic and glycolytic signature genes are persistent up to 3 days under disturbed flow.
source: Hypoxic and glycolytic signature genes are persistent up to 3 days, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.
evidence: Based on time course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: Cells subjected to disturbed flow exhibited increased glucose uptake compared to unidirectional flow as measured by 2-NBDG fluorescence.
source: Cells subjected to DF exhibited increased glucose uptake as evidenced by increased 2-NBDG fluorescence (Figure 1C and D) and 2-DG6P uptake (Figure 1E) as compared to UF.
evidence: Based on 2-NBDG fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Cells subjected to disturbed flow exhibited increased glucose uptake compared to unidirectional flow as measured by 2-DG6P uptake.
source: Cells subjected to DF exhibited increased glucose uptake as evidenced by increased 2-NBDG fluorescence (Figure 1C and D) and 2-DG6P uptake (Figure 1E) as compared to UF.
evidence: Based on 2-DG6P uptake assay shown in Figure 1E

claim: Disturbed flow increased both basal glycolysis and glycolytic capacity in HAECs compared to unidirectional flow.
source: DF increased both basal glycolysis and glycolytic capacity in HAECs as compared to UF (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Based on glycolysis stress test measurements shown in Figure 1F,G

claim: Disturbed flow reduced basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity in HAECs.
source: DF reduced basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity in HAECs (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Based on mitochondrial stress test measurements shown in Figure 1H,I

claim: Under unidirectional flow, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation accounted for approximately 17% of total ATP production.
source: Whereas under UF mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation accounted for ~17% of total ATP production, under DF mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation accounted for less than 1% of the total ATP (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Based on ATP production measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: Under disturbed flow, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation accounted for less than 1% of total ATP production.
source: Whereas under UF mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation accounted for ~17% of total ATP production, under DF mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation accounted for less than 1% of the total ATP (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Based on ATP production measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: HAECs under static conditions show an intermediate glycolytic and oxidative phenotype between disturbed flow and unidirectional flow.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A and B, HAECs under static conditions show an intermediate glycolytic and oxidative phenotype.
evidence: Based on bioenergetics measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A and B

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis predicted KLF2 as a major driver of transcriptional changes induced by unidirectional flow.
source: Based on the flow-sensitive 3757 DEGs and a priori knowledge of upstream gene regulation, IPA predicted Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2) as a major driver of transcriptional changes induced by UF, and HIF-1α driving transcriptional changes induced by DF (Figure 2A, IPA network genes for top 10 predicted upstream regulators are provided in Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on IPA analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis predicted HIF-1α as a major driver of transcriptional changes induced by disturbed flow.
source: Based on the flow-sensitive 3757 DEGs and a priori knowledge of upstream gene regulation, IPA predicted Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2) as a major driver of transcriptional changes induced by UF, and HIF-1α driving transcriptional changes induced by DF (Figure 2A, IPA network genes for top 10 predicted upstream regulators are provided in Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on IPA analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: HIF-1α protein expression was increased in disturbed flow-subjected HAECs.
source: HIF-1α protein expression was increased in DF-subjected HAECs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Disturbed flow had no effect on HIF-1α mRNA levels.
source: However, DF had no effect on HIF-1α mRNA levels (Figure 2C) suggesting that DF increases HIF-1α protein through a post-transcriptional mechanism.
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Disturbed flow increases HIF-1α protein through a post-transcriptional mechanism.
source: However, DF had no effect on HIF-1α mRNA levels (Figure 2C) suggesting that DF increases HIF-1α protein through a post-transcriptional mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that protein increases without mRNA change

claim: The disturbed flow-induced increase in HIF-1α protein levels is dynamic and reversible.
source: Furthermore, the DF-induced increase in HIF-1α protein levels was dynamic and reversible. The DF-induced increase in HIF-1α protein could be reversed by switching to UF, whereas the UF-induced reduction could be reversed by switching to DF (Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on flow-switching experiments shown in Figure 2D

claim: Transcriptome analyses identified 2989 differentially expressed genes regulated by HIF-1α in HAECs under disturbed flow.
source: Transcriptome analyses identified 2989 DEGs regulated by HIF-1α in HAECs under DF (FDR < 0.05).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis of HIF-1α knockdown under disturbed flow

claim: HIF-1α-regulated differentially expressed genes are enriched in hypoxia and glycolysis pathways.
source: GSEA (Figure 2E) and DAVID (Figure 2F) identified that HIF-1α-regulated DEGs are enriched in hypoxia and glycolysis, indicating that HIF-1α significantly contributes to the glycolytic gene signature detected in DF-treated HAECs.
evidence: Based on GSEA and DAVID analysis shown in Figure 2E and 2F

claim: HAECs exposed to disturbed flow had much higher ROS levels compared to unidirectional flow as measured by CellRox.
source: HAECs exposed to DF had much higher ROS levels as measured by CellRox, a cytoplasmic ROS indicator (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Based on CellRox fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Treatment with antioxidant EUK134 reduced HIF-1α levels in disturbed flow-treated HAECs.
source: Treating cells with an antioxidant, EUK134, a synthetic superoxide dismutase/catalase mimetic (Rong et al., 1999), reduced HIF-1α levels in DF-treated HAECs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Treatment with antioxidant EUK134 had no effect on unidirectional flow-treated HAECs.
source: Treatment with antioxidant EUK134 had no effect on UF-treated HAECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Exposure to disturbed flow increased the expression of NOX4 protein.
source: Western blot analysis showed that exposure to DF increased the expression of NOX4 protein (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Inhibition of NOX4 with siRNA reduced disturbed flow-induced ROS in HAECs.
source: Inhibition of NOX4 with siRNA reduced DF-induced ROS (Figure 3E,F) and HIF-1α levels (Figure 3G) in HAECs subjected to DF.
evidence: Based on CellRox measurements shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Inhibition of NOX4 with siRNA reduced disturbed flow-induced HIF-1α levels in HAECs.
source: Inhibition of NOX4 with siRNA reduced DF-induced ROS (Figure 3E,F) and HIF-1α levels (Figure 3G) in HAECs subjected to DF.
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3G

claim: HIF-1α reaches maximal induction at 4 hours before stabilizing at a slightly lower level under disturbed flow.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, HIF-1α is maximally induced at 4 hr before stabilizing at the levels seen at 24 hr.
evidence: Based on time course Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: NOX4 steadily accumulates over time under disturbed flow.
source: NOX4, on the other hand, steadily accumulates over time.
evidence: Based on time course Western blot data

claim: NOX4 activation by disturbed flow is required for initial induction of HIF-1α.
source: Thus, NOX4 activation by DF is required for initial induction of HIF-1α.
evidence: Based on NOX4 knockdown experiments at early time points

claim: Transcripts of 18 glycolytic enzymes were significantly increased in HAECs under disturbed flow compared to unidirectional flow.
source: Transcripts of 18 glycolytic enzymes were significantly increased (FDR < 0.05) in HAECs under DF when compared to UF and 13 of these enzymes were significantly reduced when DF induced HIF-1α was inhibited by siRNAs.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: 13 glycolytic enzymes were significantly reduced when disturbed flow-induced HIF-1α was inhibited by siRNAs.
source: Transcripts of 18 glycolytic enzymes were significantly increased (FDR < 0.05) in HAECs under DF when compared to UF and 13 of these enzymes were significantly reduced when DF induced HIF-1α was inhibited by siRNAs.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis of HIF-1α knockdown

claim: Hexokinase-2 and glucose transporter-1 were the most differentially expressed glycolytic genes at the transcription level by disturbed flow.
source: Among these DF-activated, HIF-1α-dependent genes, we found that hexokinase-2 (HK2), and glucose transporter-1 (SLC2A1/GLUT1) were the most differentially expressed at the transcription level by DF.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Disturbed flow increased the mRNA and protein expression of endothelial SLC2A1 and HK2.
source: Confirming the RNA-seq data, we found that disturbed flow increased the mRNA and protein expression of endothelial SLC2A1 and HK2 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Based on qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Transfecting HAECs with HIF-1α-targeting siRNAs reduced or prevented disturbed flow-induced SLC2A1 and HK2 mRNA and protein expressions.
source: Transfecting HAECs with HIF-1α-targeting siRNAs reduced or prevented DF-induced SLC2A1 and HK2 mRNA and protein expressions (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Based on qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: Stabilized HIF-1α mutant transfected HAECs had higher mRNA expression of SLC2A1 and HK2 compared to control.
source: Compared to control, mHIF-1α transfected HAECs had higher mRNA expression of SLC2A1 and HK2 (Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4G

claim: HIF-1α knockdown significantly reduced the basal glycolysis and glycolytic capacity in HAECs subjected to disturbed flow.
source: HIF-1α knockdown significantly reduced the basal glycolysis and glycolytic capacity in HAECs subjected to DF for 48 hr (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: Based on glycolysis stress test data shown in Figure 4H,I

claim: EPAS1 (HIF-2α) is increased under disturbed flow.
source: To assess whether EPAS1 (HIF-2α) contributes to the glycolytic phenotype under DF, as EPAS1 is also predicted to be a transcriptional regulator from IPA (Figure 2A), we first verified that EPAS1 was increased under DF (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: EPAS1 inhibition did not result in statistically significant reduction in glycolytic genes HK2 and SLC2A1 in cells under disturbed flow.
source: however, there was no statistically significant reduction in glycolytic genes HK2 and SLC2A1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) as the result of EPAS1 inhibition in cells under DF.
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: HIF-1α but not EPAS1 (HIF-2α) is required for the disturbed flow-induced increase in glycolytic enzymes.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that HIF-1α but not EPAS1 (HIF-2α) is required for the DF-induced increase in two of the most highly transcriptionally regulated glycolytic enzymes.
evidence: Based on comparison of HIF-1α and EPAS1 knockdown effects

claim: HIF-1α knockdown reversed the disturbed flow-induced reduction in maximal respiratory capacity.
source: HIF-1α knockdown reversed the DF-induced reduction in maximal respiratory capacity (Figure 5A), and increased the basal oxygen consumption and reserve respiratory capacity (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on mitochondrial stress test data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: HIF-1α knockdown increased the basal oxygen consumption and reserve respiratory capacity under disturbed flow.
source: HIF-1α knockdown reversed the DF-induced reduction in maximal respiratory capacity (Figure 5A), and increased the basal oxygen consumption and reserve respiratory capacity (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on mitochondrial stress test data shown in Figure 5B

claim: No difference was noted in mitochondria density by MitoTracker staining between disturbed flow and unidirectional flow.
source: In HAECs subjected to either DF or UF for 48 hr, no difference was noted in mitochondria density by MitoTracker staining, a surrogate for mitochondria mass (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) (Agnello et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on MitoTracker staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: There was no difference in transcript levels of mitochondrially encoded genes ND-1 and ND-5 under athero-relevant flows.
source: Furthermore, there was also no difference in transcript levels of mitochondrially encoded genes such as NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase chain 1 (ND-1) and 5 (ND-5) under athero-relevant flows (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Glucose oxidation contributes to 43% of the total oxygen consumption rate under unidirectional flow.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 5C, glucose oxidation (as estimated by UK5099 treatment) contributes to 43% of the total oxygen consumption rate under UF but confers 62% of total OCR under DF.
evidence: Based on substrate utilization measurements shown in Figure 5C

claim: Glucose oxidation confers 62% of total oxygen consumption rate under disturbed flow.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 5C, glucose oxidation (as estimated by UK5099 treatment) contributes to 43% of the total oxygen consumption rate under UF but confers 62% of total OCR under DF.
evidence: Based on substrate utilization measurements shown in Figure 5C

claim: PDK1 was the only pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase gene that is upregulated by disturbed flow in the RNA-seq data.
source: Among the 4 PDK genes (PDK1-4) expressed in HAECs, PDK1 was the only one that is upregulated by DF in the RNA-seq data.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Disturbed flow increased PDK1 mRNA and protein expression.
source: Consistent with these data, DF increased PDK1 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and protein expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5D

claim: Loss of HIF-1α in HAECs attenuated disturbed flow-induced upregulation of PDK1 mRNA and protein.
source: Loss of HIF-1α in HAECs attenuated DF-induced upregulation of PDK1 mRNA (Figure 5E) and protein (Figure 5F).
evidence: Based on qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 5E,F

claim: Disturbed flow increased pyruvate dehydrogenase activity compared to unidirectional flow.
source: Consistent with the increased PDK1 expression, DF increased PDH activity compared to UF (Figure 5G).
evidence: Based on PDH activity assay shown in Figure 5G

claim: HIF-1α knockdown showed partial reversal of the disturbed flow-induced reduction of PDH activity.
source: Studies in HAECs with HIF-1α knockdown and PDK1 knockdown showed partial (Figure 5H) and complete reversal (Figure 5I) of the DF-induced reduction of PDH activity, respectively.
evidence: Based on PDH activity assay shown in Figure 5H

claim: PDK1 knockdown showed complete reversal of the disturbed flow-induced reduction of PDH activity.
source: Studies in HAECs with HIF-1α knockdown and PDK1 knockdown showed partial (Figure 5H) and complete reversal (Figure 5I) of the DF-induced reduction of PDH activity, respectively.
evidence: Based on PDH activity assay shown in Figure 5I

claim: PDK1 inhibition with dichloroacetate partially rescued the reduced maximal respiration and respiratory capacity induced by disturbed flow.
source: PDK1 inhibition partially rescued the reduced maximal respiration and respiratory capacity induced by DF (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: Based on mitochondrial stress test data shown in Figure 5J–K

claim: Genetic inhibition of PDK1 expression by siRNA partially rescued the reduced maximal respiration and respiratory capacity induced by disturbed flow.
source: Similar results were obtained with genetic inhibition of PDK1 expression by siRNA (Figure 5L–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on mitochondrial stress test data shown in Figure 5L–M

claim: Under disturbed flow, HIF-1α promotes PDK1 expression to reduce the entry of glucose-derived pyruvate into the TCA cycle.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that under DF, HIF-1α promotes PDK1 expression to reduce the entry of glucose-derived pyruvate into the TCA cycle, and consequently limits mitochondrial reserve function.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of HIF-1α and PDK1 experiments

claim: Exposure of HAECs to disturbed flow for 48 hours resulted in increased expression of pro-inflammatory genes including VCAM-1, IL8 and CCL2 compared to unidirectional flow.
source: Exposure of HAECs to DF for 48 hr resulted in increased expression of pro-inflammatory genes including VCAM-1, IL8 and CCL2 compared to UF (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA reduced disturbed flow-induced expression of IL8, VCAM-1, and CCL2.
source: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA reduced DF-induced expression of IL8, VCAM-1, and CCL2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Knocking down HIF-1α under disturbed flow reduced the binding of monocytes (THP-1) to the HAECs.
source: Knocking down HIF-1α under disturbed flow also reduced the binding of monocytes (THP-1) to the HAECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on leukocyte adhesion assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Ectopic expression of stabilized HIF-1α increased IL8, VCAM-1, and CCL2 expression in HAECs.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of stabilized HIF-1α, like DF, increased IL8, VCAM-1, and CCL2 expression in HAECs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6C

claim: siRNA-mediated NOX4 inhibition reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes in disturbed flow-treated HAECs.
source: Moreover, siRNA-mediated NOX4 inhibition, which prevented the DF-induced HIF-1α, reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes in DF-treated HAECs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Inhibition of SLC2A1 reduced disturbed flow-induced VCAM-1 and CCL2 gene expression.
source: Inhibition of SLC2A1 (or glycolysis) reduced DF-induced VCAM-1 and CCL2 gene expression (Figure 6E).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Inhibition of PDK1 significantly reduced inflammatory gene expression under disturbed flow.
source: To rescue the DF-induced reduction in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, we treated HAECs with siRNA against PDK1. Inhibition of PDK1 also significantly reduced inflammatory gene expression (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Inhibition of the electron transport chain with rotenone and antimycin increased IL8, VCAM1, and CCL2 in unidirectional flow.
source: We found that inhibition of the electron transport chain with rotenone and antimycin increased IL8, VCAM1, and CCL2 in UF (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: Disturbed flow-induced metabolic reprogramming (induction of glycolysis and inhibition of mitochondrial oxidation) is required for the disturbed flow-induced pro-inflammatory phenotype.
source: In summary, these findings suggest that DF-induced metabolic reprogramming; namely induction of glycolysis and inhibition of mitochondrial oxidation, is required for the DF-induced pro-inflammatory phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of metabolic and inflammatory gene expression experiments

claim: Disturbed flow causes increased phosphorylation of the p65 subunit of NF-κB.
source: Indeed, we found that DF causes increased phosphorylation of the p65 subunit of NF-κB (Figure 6G).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Knock down of HIF-1α reduced disturbed flow-induced NF-κB activation.
source: Knock down HIF-1α reduced DF-induced NF-κB activation (Figure 6H).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Pretreatment of NBD prevented the HIF-1α-induced increase in inflammation.
source: Pretreatment of NBD prevented the HIF-1α-induced increase in inflammation (Figure 6I).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6I

claim: Pretreatment of HAECs with NBD prior to disturbed flow did not affect disturbed flow-induced increase in HIF-1α levels.
source: Pretreatment of HAECs with NBD prior to 24 hr of DF did not affect DF-induced increase in HIF-1α levels, suggesting that NF-κB activation is not responsible for HIF-1α stabilization in HAECs under DF (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4

claim: NF-κB activation is not responsible for HIF-1α stabilization in HAECs under disturbed flow.
source: Pretreatment of HAECs with NBD prior to 24 hr of DF did not affect DF-induced increase in HIF-1α levels, suggesting that NF-κB activation is not responsible for HIF-1α stabilization in HAECs under DF (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NF-κB inhibition does not affect HIF-1α levels

claim: KLF2 was downregulated 11-fold under disturbed flow when compared to unidirectional flow.
source: In our RNAseq dataset, KLF2 was downregulated 11-fold under DF when compared to UF (FDR < 0.000345).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Knockdown of HIF-1α under disturbed flow increased KLF2 levels.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A, knockdown of HIF-1α under DF increased KLF2 levels (but not KLF4) (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A

claim: Disturbed flow-induced metabolic changes driven by HIF-1α cause increased inflammation through an NF-κB-dependent mechanism.
source: Together, these results suggest that DF-induced metabolic changes driven by HIF-1α cause increased inflammation through an NF-κB-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of HIF-1α, metabolic, and NF-κB experiments

claim: The inner curvature of the aortic arch is constantly exposed to disturbed flow and prone to atherosclerosis.
source: The inner curvature of the aortic arch is constantly exposed to DF, and prone to atherosclerosis while the nearby descending thoracic aorta is subjected to UF, and resistant to atherosclerosis (Figure 7A).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The descending thoracic aorta is subjected to unidirectional flow and resistant to atherosclerosis.
source: The inner curvature of the aortic arch is constantly exposed to DF, and prone to atherosclerosis while the nearby descending thoracic aorta is subjected to UF, and resistant to atherosclerosis (Figure 7A).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Endothelia located in aortic arch exhibited cobblestone morphology and greater amounts of ROS compared to elongated endothelia in the nearby descending aorta.
source: En face images showed that endothelia located in aortic arch exhibited cobblestone morphology and greater amounts of ROS (measured by dihydroethidium bromide) (Figure 7B) compared to elongated endothelia in the nearby descending aorta (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on en face imaging and ROS measurements shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: Endothelia isolated from the inner curvature of swine aortic arch showed significantly increased protein expression of NOX4, HIF-1α, glycolytic enzymes SLC2A1, HK2, PDK1, and phospho-p65 compared to those isolated from descending thoracic aorta.
source: As shown in Figure 7D and E, we detected significantly increased protein expression of NOX4, HIF-1α and glycolytic enzymes SLC2A1, HK2, and PDK1, as well as phosho-p65, in endothelia isolated form the inner curvature of swine aortic arch as compared to those isolated from descending thoracic aorta in the same animal.
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 7D,E

claim: NOX4 was increased in parts of murine aortas exposed to disturbed flow.
source: Similarly, using immunofluorescence, we confirmed that NOX4 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B) and HIF-1α were increased in parts of murine aortas, after live perfusion with fixative followed by immunofluorescence (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: HIF-1α was increased in parts of murine aortas exposed to disturbed flow.
source: Similarly, using immunofluorescence, we confirmed that NOX4 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B) and HIF-1α were increased in parts of murine aortas, after live perfusion with fixative followed by immunofluorescence (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: In vivo results are consistent with in vitro studies demonstrating that disturbed flow promotes endothelial glycolytic metabolism and reduced mitochondrial function by increasing NOX4-mediated ROS production and consequent HIF-1α stabilization.
source: These in vivo results are consistent with the in vitro studies demonstrating that disturbed flow promotes endothelial glycolytic metabolism and reduced mitochondrial function by increasing NOX4-mediated ROS production and consequent HIF-1α stabilization.
evidence: Inferred from the consistency between in vitro and in vivo results

claim: Disturbed flow increases endothelial glycolysis and reduces mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation by promoting NOX4-dependent ROS-mediated HIF-1α stabilization.
source: We found that DF increases endothelial glycolysis and reduces mitochondrial respiratory capacity by promoting NOX4-dependent ROS-mediated HIF-1α stabilization.
evidence: Stated as a major finding from the study

claim: NOX4, ROS, HIF-1α, and key glycolytic activators were increased in vivo in endothelial cells isolated from the inner curvatures of porcine aortic arch compared to nearby descending thoracic aorta.
source: In agreement with the in vitro investigations, NOX4, ROS, HIF-1α, and key glycolytic activators were also increased in vivo in endothelial cells isolated from the inner curvatures of porcine aortic arch, which represents an area where cells are exposed to DF when compared to nearby descending thoracic aorta where cells are subjected to UF.
evidence: Based on in vivo measurements in porcine aorta

claim: A metabolic switch comprising HIF-1α-dependent reduction in respiratory capacity and increased glycolysis are important molecular signatures that characterize the athero-susceptible endothelium associated with disturbed flow.
source: These findings demonstrate that a metabolic switch comprising HIF-1α-dependent reduction in respiratory capacity and increased glycolysis as important molecular signatures that characterize the athero-susceptible endothelium associated with DF.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: KLF2 and HIF-1α are the major transcriptional regulators that control the endothelial phenotypes related to athero-relevant flows.
source: Our RNA-seq analyses predicted that KLF2 and HIF-1α are the major transcriptional regulators that control the endothelial phenotypes related to athero-relevant flows.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq and IPA analysis

claim: Disturbed flow-induced expression of HIF-1α promotes endothelial glycolytic metabolism and reduces mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Subsequent mechanistic investigations further demonstrate that DF-induced expression of HIF-1α promotes endothelial glycolytic metabolism and reduces mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Stated as a mechanistic finding from the study

claim: Glycolysis plays a central role in the promotion of angiogenesis.
source: Our data are consistent with reports on glycolysis playing a central role in the promotion of angiogenesis (De Bock et al., 2013b; Potente et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Bock et al., 2013b; Potente et al., 2011

claim: HIF-1α is expressed in all cells of all metazoan species.
source: While HIF-1α is expressed in all cells of all metazoan species, HIF-2α is only expressed in certain cell types of vertebrate species including endothelial cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: HIF-2α is only expressed in certain cell types of vertebrate species including endothelial cells.
source: While HIF-1α is expressed in all cells of all metazoan species, HIF-2α is only expressed in certain cell types of vertebrate species including endothelial cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: HIF-1α controls the expression of multiple gene products that mediate glycolysis.
source: Unlike HIF-2α, HIF-1α controls the expression of multiple gene products that mediate glycolysis (Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012

claim: HIF-1α activates transcription of PDK1, which phosphorylates and inactivates the catalytic subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase.
source: For instance, HIF-1α activates transcription of PDK1, which phosphorylates and inactivates the catalytic subunit of PDH, the enzyme that converts glucose-derived pyruvate into acetyl-CoA for entry into the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2006

claim: Besides PDK1, HIF-1α exerts its effects on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation via additional signaling pathways.
source: These findings indicate that besides PDK1, HIF-1α exerts its effects on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation via additional signaling pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PDK1 inhibition only partially restores mitochondrial function

claim: Increased LDHA is predicted to reduce the availability of pyruvate to enter the TCA cycle and hence limit the substrate availability for oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Increased LDHA is predicted to reduce the availability of pyruvate to enter the TCA cycle and hence limit the substrate availability for oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on LDHA function

claim: NOX4-dependent ROS is a major contributor to promote disturbed flow-induced HIF-1α stabilization.
source: Our results identified NOX4-dependent ROS as a major contributor to promote DF-induced HIF-1α stabilization.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the study

claim: Oscillatory flow increases NOX4 expression and ROS production in cultured bovine aortic endothelial cells.
source: The data are consistent with a previous study showing that oscillatory flow increases NOX4 expression and ROS production in cultured bovine aortic endothelial cells (Hwang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hwang et al., 2003

claim: Increased NOX4 expression and ROS generation, accompanied by elevated HIF-1α, were detected in vivo in endothelia isolated from the athero-susceptible swine aortic arch.
source: In agreement with these in vitro investigations, we detected increased NOX4 expression and ROS generation, accompanied by elevated HIF-1α, in vivo in endothelia isolated from the athero-susceptible swine aortic arch.
evidence: Based on in vivo measurements in swine aorta

claim: ROS are known to stabilize HIF-1α even in normoxic conditions.
source: ROS are known to stabilize HIF-1α even in normoxic conditions (Bonello et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bonello et al., 2007

claim: HIF-1α stabilization has been shown to occur in stretch-based assays by stretch-induced inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase.
source: HIF-1α stabilization has also been shown to occur in stretch-based assays by stretch-induced inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase, and is thought to mediate epithelial protection during ventilator-induced lung injury (Eckle et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eckle et al., 2013, 2014

claim: Flow by itself is unlikely to cause mechanical stretch in either the in vitro assays or in the aorta in vivo.
source: While it is possible that accumulation of mitochondrial TCA substrates contributes to HIF-1α stabilization under DF, flow by itself is unlikely to cause mechanical stretch in either the in vitro assays or in the aorta in vivo, as UF is more likely than DF to cause stretch (UF has 10-fold higher shear stress compared to DF).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of shear stress between UF and DF

claim: HIF-1α mRNA increases after prolonged stretch in rat skeletal muscle capillary beds.
source: HIF-1α mRNA is also thought to increase after prolonged stretch in rat skeletal muscle capillary beds (Milkiewicz et al., 2007; Milkiewicz and Haas, 2005) and the inferior vena cava (Lim et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milkiewicz et al., 2007; Milkiewicz and Haas, 2005; Lim et al., 2011

claim: Disturbed flow-induced endothelial metabolic reprogramming contributes to increased inflammatory gene expression.
source: Another major finding of the present study is the demonstration that DF-induced endothelial metabolic reprogramming contributes to increased inflammatory gene expression.
evidence: Stated as a major finding from the study

claim: Disturbed flow-induced expression of pro-inflammatory genes was markedly attenuated with the knockdown of SLC2A1, PDK1, or HIF-1α.
source: DF-induced expression of pro-inflammatory genes was markedly attenuated with the knockdown of SLC2A1, PDK1, or HIF-1α (loss-of-function), and increased by HIF-1α overexpression (gain-of-function).
evidence: Based on loss-of-function experiments

claim: HIF-1α overexpression increased pro-inflammatory gene expression.
source: DF-induced expression of pro-inflammatory genes was markedly attenuated with the knockdown of SLC2A1, PDK1, or HIF-1α (loss-of-function), and increased by HIF-1α overexpression (gain-of-function).
evidence: Based on gain-of-function experiments

claim: Increased HIF-1α, SLC2A1, and PDK1 expression were detected in vivo in swine aortic arch endothelial cells.
source: Corroborating our in vitro results, we detected increased HIF-1α, SLC2A1, and PDK1 expression in vivo in swine aortic arch ECs.
evidence: Based on in vivo measurements in swine aorta

claim: HIF-1α expression is increased in carotid artery plaques.
source: These results are in agreement with the reported increase in the expression of HIF-1α in carotid artery plaques (Vink et al., 2007; Sluimer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vink et al., 2007; Sluimer et al., 2008

claim: Aortic arch endothelial cells exposed to disturbed flow in vivo exhibit NF-κB activation.
source: Aortic arch ECs have exposed to DF in vivo also been shown to exhibit NF-κB activation (Hajra et al., 2000; Fang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hajra et al., 2000; Fang et al., 2010

claim: Increased glycolysis may promote endothelial inflammation via lactate-induced activation of NF-κB signaling.
source: Although the underlying molecular mechanisms remain to be elucidated, one possibility is that increased glycolysis promotes endothelial inflammation via lactate-induced activation of NF-κB signaling in a manner described in immune cells such as macrophages (Végran et al., 2011; Covarrubias et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to Végran et al., 2011; Covarrubias et al., 2015

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α in disturbed flow-treated endothelial cells rescued the expression of anti-inflammatory molecules KLF2, KLF4, and PPAP2B.
source: For example, our RNA-seq analyses demonstrated that inhibition of HIF-1α in DF-treated ECs rescued the expression of anti-inflammatory molecules KLF2, KLF4, and PPAP2B (a coronary arterial disease candidate gene identified by genome-wide association studies) (SenBanerjee et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: KLF2 is required for unidirectional flow-induced reduction in the expression of glycolytic genes in human umbilical vein endothelial cells.
source: While we did not study the role of KLF2, Doddaballapur et al. showed that KLF2 is required for UF-induced reduction in the expression of glycolytic genes in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (Doddaballapur et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doddaballapur et al., 2015

claim: Inflammatory stimuli such as TNFα can reduce the unidirectional flow-responsiveness of KLF2.
source: Importantly, Inflammatory stimuli such as TNFα can by itself reduce the UF-responsiveness of KLF2 (Huang et al., 2017); it remains to be seen if metabolic changes might also play a role under such stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2017

claim: Differential flow waveforms may amplify endothelial cell metabolic phenotypes by providing transcriptional mechanisms to increase glycolysis and reduce respiration under disturbed flow and to reduce glycolysis and increase respiration under unidirectional flow.
source: Thus, differential flow waveforms may amplify EC metabolic phenotypes (and subsequent pro- or anti-inflammatory states) by providing transcriptional mechanisms to increase glycolysis and reduce respiration under DF and to reduce glycolysis and increase respiration under UF.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on study findings

claim: Spatial inhibition of glycolytic metabolism and HIF-1α signaling may be a suitable approach for future arterial wall-based therapies that target disturbed flow-activated endothelium associated with focal atherosclerosis.
source: Our in vitro and in vivo results suggest spatial inhibition of glycolytic metabolism and HIF-1α signaling may be a suitable approach for future arterial wall-based therapies that target disturbed flow-activated endothelium associated with focal atherosclerosis.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on study findings

claim: Endothelium-deletion of HIF-1α significantly ameliorated atherosclerotic burden in apoe−/− mice.
source: Consistent with the results demonstrating HIF-1α inhibition reduces the disturbed flow-induced inflammation, endothelium-deletion of HIF-1α was recently shown to significantly ameliorate atherosclerotic burden in apoe−/− mice (Akhtar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Akhtar et al., 2015

claim: Metabolic plasticity of endothelium is dynamically and reversibly regulated by hemodynamics.
source: Here, we described that metabolic plasticity of endothelium is dynamically and reversibly regulated by hemodynamics suggesting a critical role for mechanical forces in actively mediating metabolic changes that drive endothelial functions in health and disease.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings
